name: Timor-Leste
summary_text: Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex sexual conduct. Same-sex sexual acts have been legal since 1975, and no source records anti-trans legislation, arrest patterns, or police targeting of trans people in the country. No law restricting trans people from public facilities, health care, or employment is documented.  No legal gender recognition procedure exists in Timor-Leste. For a visitor, the operative document is therefore the passport or identity card issued in the home jurisdiction, including any gender marker changed there. There is no domestic route by which a foreign trans person could alter or regularise a marker while in the country.  Official signals run in a supportive direction at the highest level. The Prime Minister gave televised endorsement to the country's first Pride parade in 2017, and President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the 2019 march, stating that he is a president for all people. Day-to-day rejection is nonetheless documented alongside those statements, including hostile messages sent to the family of a Pride organiser, so public visibility attracts both state endorsement and social hostility.  Pride marches are held annually in Dili, in July. A visitor present during those weeks can expect a visible public event of a scale that has grown substantially since 2017.

name: Tunisia
summary_text: Tunisia criminalises same-sex conduct under Penal Code Article 230, which carries up to three years' imprisonment, and enforcement is active rather than dormant. Article 226 bis on public indecency is applied to gender expression, and enforcement of both provisions falls disproportionately on transgender women. In October 2021 two transgender women were arrested under morality and debauchery provisions.  The scale of the current campaign is documented by Amnesty International on 11 February 2025: at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. The arrests took place in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, so the sweep is national in character rather than confined to one city. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years; the convictions were upheld on appeal on 5 February 2025, with four people released only after sentence reduction.  Human Rights Watch recorded at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months in 2016, all convicted under Article 230. Detainees interviewed in those cases reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police, which places physical abuse by the security services inside the ordinary arrest process rather than outside it.  Tunisia pledged to the United Nations in 2017 to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases while retaining the anti-gay law itself, so the commitment changed examination practice without decriminalising anything. A visitor should not read that pledge as a change in exposure to prosecution.  Legal gender recognition is unsettled and frequently refused. In April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man, weighing contradictory lower-court judgements, including case No. 12304/2018, and finding no consistent precedent; the question remains unresolved below the Court of Cassation, which makes recognition a court-by-court gamble. Cairo 52 records that gaps persist in legal gender recognition generally.  Custody carries documented identity risk. The Intersection Association reported in November 2024 that transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, a systemic refusal of identity from the point of detention onward and a source of continuous suffering inside the prison system. A trans visitor who is detained should expect documents and hearings to use a name and gender marker they do not recognise.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch - 6 July 2020 statement on sentencing
sources.documents: Documented incident: Tunisian court sentenced two men for homosexuality; arrested 3 June on suspicion of same-sex conduct; police attempted anal exam as evidence; related practice where refusal viewed as guilt and June 2017 case of 16-year-old sentenced to four months after refusing exam
sources.detail: Cited in text as 'On 6 July 2020, Human Rights Watch said that a Tunisian court sentenced two men for homosexuality. Police arrested the two men on the suspicion of same-sex conduct on 3 June and attempted to subject the defendants to an anal exam'. No URL visible.

sources.title: Individual Freedoms and Equality Committee (COLIBE) - Report to President Beji Caid Essebsi, 15 June 2018
